extracted.intended_audience: people of the State of New York; citizens and voters considering ratification of the U.S. Constitution (readers seeking principles for structuring the federal judiciary)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance on what categories of cases the federal judiciary should hear, how judicial power should be distributed between Supreme and inferior courts, and institutional safeguards (tenure, independence, appellate/original jurisdiction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper objects of the federal judicature (enumerated classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The judiciary authority of the Union ought to extend to: (1) all cases arising out of the laws of the United States, passed in pursuance of their constitutional powers; (2) all those which concern the execution of the provisions expressly contained in the articles of Union; (3) all those in which the United States are a party; (4) all those which involve the peace of the confederacy, whether they relate to intercourse between the United States and foreign nations, or between the States themselves; (5) all those which originate on the high seas, and are of admiralty or maritime jurisdiction; and lastly, to all those in which the State tribunals cannot be supposed to be impartial and unbiased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton explains each class with examples and reasons: enforcement of prohibitions (e.g., duties on imports, emission of paper money) requires federal adjudication; uniformity in interpreting national laws prevents contradiction; controversies involving the nation require national tribunals; cases implicating foreign parties/treaties and admiralty affect public peace; and instances of state-partiality (e.g., land grants conflicting across states) mandate federal cognizance. The list is presented as the 'entire mass' of the Union's judicial authority and is a foundational checklist for what federal courts should cover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional method to give efficacy to constitutional provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: There ought always to be a constitutional method of giving efficacy to constitutional provisions — prohibitions on State legislatures must have some effectual power in the government to restrain or correct infractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton contrasts two means: a direct negative on state laws versus authority in federal courts to overrule state laws that contravene the articles of Union, and notes the convention preferred federal judicial authority. Example infractions: duties on imported articles, emission of paper money. This functions as a criterion for designing remedies and enforcement mechanisms in a federal system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial power coextensive with legislative power for uniform interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The propriety of the judicial power of a government being coextensive with its legislative may be ranked among political axioms — the mere necessity of uniformity in the interpretation of the national laws decides the question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton warns against multiple independent final courts interpreting the same laws (thirteen final courts would create contradiction). This is a design principle: where a legislature enacts national laws, there must be a national judiciary with competence to interpret them uniformly.

rubrics_metrics.name: National tribunals for controversies between the nation and its members/citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: Controversies between the nation and its members or citizens can only be properly referred to the national tribunals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton treats this as obvious and necessary: only national courts suit disputes where the United States itself is a party; any other plan would be contrary to reason, precedent, and decorum. This is a jurisdictional rule for case-allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal cognizance of cases involving foreigners, treaties, and laws of nations
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal judiciary ought to have cognizance of all causes in which the citizens of other countries are concerned — essential to preservation of the public faith and the security of public tranquillity; cases arising upon treaties and the laws of nations are proper for federal jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton notes the practical impossibility of discriminating between treaty/ international-law cases and purely municipal-law cases involving foreigners; because many cases with foreign parties implicate national questions, safest to refer all such to national tribunals. An unjust sentence against a foreigner might be an aggression on his sovereign; federal courts protect national responsibility to foreign powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal jurisdiction over disputes between States and between states and out-of-state citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of determining causes between two States, between one State and the citizens of another, and between the citizens of different States is essential to the peace of the Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton invokes historical examples (German territorial dissensions) and argues for a federal forum to terminate territorial disputes, check fraudulent state laws that disturb harmony, and supervise practices disturbing inter-state relations. This is a stability-preserving jurisdictional criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal authority to secure privileges and immunities equality
rubrics_metrics.description: To secure the inviolable maintenance of equality of privileges and immunities of citizens of each State, the national judiciary ought to preside in all cases where one State or its citizens are opposed to another State or its citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton emphasizes impartiality: a tribunal without local attachments, owing existence to the Union, is best positioned to construe the privileges-and-immunities clause and prevent local evasion or subterfuge. This is a criterion for assigning cases where equality across States is implicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admiralty and maritime jurisdiction belongs to federal courts
rubrics_metrics.description: The most important part of maritime causes are, by the present Confederation, submitted to federal jurisdiction; admiralty and maritime causes generally depend on the laws of nations and commonly affect rights of foreigners, so they fall within considerations relative to public peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton notes broad consensus on placing maritime causes in national courts; this supports a rule that admiralty matters be federally adjudicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal jurisdiction where state tribunals cannot be impartial (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where State tribunals cannot be supposed impartial — e.g., claims to land under grants of different States founded upon adverse pretensions of boundary — federal tribunals should determine such controversies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton explains that State courts might be prejudiced (laws favoring the granting State) or judges naturally biased in favor of their government; federal courts prevent 'no man a judge in his own cause' conflicts. This is a practical criterion for identifying cases that require national adjudication to ensure fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of equity jurisdiction in federal courts
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal judiciary should extend 'to all cases in law and equity arising under the Constitution and the laws of the United States' because many subjects of litigation involve fraud, trust, accident, or hardship that render them equitable rather than legal in character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton gives examples: relief against 'hard bargains,' agreements to convey lands claimed under different state grants; equitable powers are necessary especially where foreigners are concerned. Where States do not maintain formal distinctions, this may be less palpable, but equity jurisdiction is nevertheless necessary for full justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: One supreme court of final jurisdiction (distinct from legislature)
rubrics_metrics.description: There ought to be one court of supreme and final jurisdiction; it should be a distinct and independent body rather than a branch of the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton counters objections that a separate Supreme Court is unprecedented or dangerous: he argues separation of departments, judges' specialized knowledge, permanence to resist legislative partisanship, and avoids perverse incentives if legislators were final judges. He cites State constitutions that vested ultimate judicial power in independent bodies as precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence and tenure (good behavior) as institutional safeguard
rubrics_metrics.description: The tenure of good behavior for judicial offices and selection of judges for their knowledge of law are necessary to prevent legislative intermixture and to secure impartial, learned decision-making; judges should not be chosen for limited periods in ways that erode independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton argues judges with permanent standing are better suited for law knowledge and to resist partisan pressures; this supports lifetime (or good-behavior) tenure rather than short, mutable legislative appointments. This is presented as a humane and practical safeguard for administering justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of Congress to constitute inferior federal courts
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress should have the power to ordain and establish inferior courts to prevent the necessity of recourse to the Supreme Court in every federal case and to enable tribunals competent to national jurisdiction within States or larger districts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton explains reasons for creating district/federal courts (e.g., forming four to half-dozen districts, instituting a federal court in each district, judges holding circuits with State judges) to administer justice with ease and despatch and to circumscribe appeals. He rejects the idea that this power intends to abolish county courts, clarifying that 'tribunals inferior to the Supreme Court' may be local or district-level federal courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of original and appellate jurisdiction between Supreme and inferior courts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court should have original jurisdiction only in cases affecting ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, and those in which a State shall be a party; all other federal cognizance should have original jurisdiction in inferior tribunals with the Supreme Court exercising appellate jurisdiction 'both as to law and fact' subject to exceptions and regulations by Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton details the rationale: public ministers represent sovereigns and cases involving them or States demand highest judicature promptly; limiting Supreme original jurisdiction keeps most business in inferior courts while preserving final appellate review. The appellate jurisdiction is broad to allow review appropriate to civil-law and common-law modes of decision, but Congress may regulate its extent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate jurisdiction both as to law and fact (subject to legislative regulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court's appellate jurisdiction is to extend both as to law and fact (the power to review proceedings of inferior tribunals 'either as to law or fact, or both'), but this jurisdiction shall be subject to exceptions and regulations the national legislature may prescribe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton explains that 'appellate' in different States has different technical senses; the federal design requires flexibility so that re-examination of fact can be allowed in some cases (e.g., prize causes) or limited in others. Congress can regulate whether re-examination involves another jury, remand, or review on the record. This is a design criterion balancing review powers and preservation of jury trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate review need not abolish jury trial; methods to preserve jury fact-finding
rubrics_metrics.description: The re-examination of a fact once ascertained by a jury will not necessarily be permitted in the Supreme Court; if re-examination is admitted it may be regulated so as to be done by a second jury, by remanding the cause to the court below for a second trial, or by directing an issue immediately out of the Supreme Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton rebuts fears that appellate jurisdiction will abolish trial by jury, stating the legislature may provide that appeals to the Supreme Court exclude re-examination of facts tried by juries, or limit re-examination to causes determinable at common law in that mode. This gives concrete options for preserving jury function while allowing appellate oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative inability to reverse judicial sentences in particular cases; limits on legislative overruling
rubrics_metrics.description: A legislature cannot reverse a judicial sentence once made in a particular case without exceeding its province; it may prescribe a new rule for future cases but cannot substitute a remedy for a specific past judicial determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton uses this principle to counter claims that legislative bodies (e.g., Parliament or State legislatures) can correct courts' erroneous decisions by law. The principle supports judicial finality in particular cases and clarifies the nature of constitutional checks and remedies (legislatures can alter future rules but cannot reverse past judicial decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Impeachment power as constitutional check on judiciary
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitutional check on judicial misconduct is the power of instituting impeachments in one part of the legislature and determining them in the other; this affords a complete security against judicial usurpations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton asserts impeachment (House to institute, Senate to try) would deter judges from extensive usurpations because the legislature possesses means to punish and remove them. This is presented as a counterbalance to fears of unaccountable federal judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent jurisdiction of State and subordinate federal courts in many federal cases
rubrics_metrics.description: States will have concurrent jurisdiction with the subordinate federal judicatories in many cases of federal cognizance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton notes (and defers detailed explanation) that concurrent jurisdiction is expected in numerous federal matters; the presence of federal inferior courts does not entirely preclude State court participation, but the extent of appeals and the distribution of original jurisdiction should be arranged to avoid excessive appeals. This is a procedural design point for case-allocation between state and federal forums.
